As you know, we need to continue the hearing of a witness called by the Prosecution -- or rather, an archivist who will be testifying today and tomorrow. Last Friday, we delayed the admission of documents so that both the Defence and the Prosecution may have a complete list of the exhibits for which admission will be requested. So last week, my colleague produced two binders containing documents divided into seven themes, and also seven additional documents were used which were not in the binders. The first document, therefore, Mr. President, is a document dated the 31st of December 1992. It is a reply on the part of a certain Blaskic addressed to the commander of the 3rd Corps. And this document was distributed to all the parties last Friday. For this document, we would like it to be admitted into evidence, though that is not possible straight away because we don't have a translation. So to begin with, we would like this document of the 31st of December to be marked for identification until we are able to provide a translation of that document. I will continue, Mr. President, with new documents. There are then four documents of the European Community Monitoring Mission. Those documents dated the 22nd of April; another one of the 22nd of April; a third is dated the 28th of April; and finally a document dated the 23rd of May 1993. For these four documents, as they are official documents emanating from the ECMM, and since these documents were recognised by the witness and he referred to the events discussed in these four documents, we would request a final exhibit number for them. In the first case, it is a request for clarification coming from the 3rd Corps; and in the second case, it is a response coming from the Operational Group East addressed to the 3rd Corps. utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, you were going too fast. We'll deal with theme number VII now. And we only have five documents left. So rest reassured. Under theme Number VII, Defence is requesting that four documents be marked for identification, one document should be given a final number. If the Defence refers to number 66, document number 66, please don't mention the name that is referred to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. After having discussed the matter and re-examined the transcript, the Defence would like the five documents under theme VII be definitively admitted. These are documents 4, 6, 11, 14, and 15. As far as Document 15 is concerned, under number 66, this is an interview that the witness recognised. He agreed to having this interview himself. As far as the first four documents are concerned, these are documents that we discussed with the witness, and the witness recognised them. He was able to discuss the context. These documents were also used to show what the witness's position was with regard to the situation in 1993 with regard to the mujahedin in Central Bosnia. And this is why, Mr. President, we would like these five documents to be given final numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have five numbers for these documents which are listed under theme VII.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document dated the 19th of July 1993 gets Exhibit Number DH269, and its English translation gets Exhibit Number 269/E. The document dated the 2nd of August 1993 gets Exhibit Number DH270, and its English translation gets the Exhibit Number DH270/E. The document dated the 28th of November 1993 gets the Exhibit Number DH271, and its English translation gets the Exhibit Number DH271/E. The document dated the 26th of February 1994 gets the Exhibit Number DH242, and its English translation gets the Exhibit Number DH -- I apologise. It was DH272. And the English translation gets Exhibit Number DH272/E. The document dated the 22nd of October 2001 gets the Exhibit Number DH273, under seal. And the English translation gets the Exhibit Number DH273/E, confidential under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have completed this numbering which can sometimes be fatiguing. But it has to be done. And I wish to thank the Defence for drafting these tables which has allowed the Registrar to provide us with the numbers. I also thank the Prosecution. In their concern to show wisdom, they did not object to the admission of these documents, all of which are official documents. We are now going to go on to another subject --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just before we move on, if I could just mention in relation to the admissability of documents. As Your Honours will know, we introduced three documents last week, two are marked for identification because the witness couldn't identify them, one which we did identify from his signature. And that leads me to making a brief, general point on the admissibility of documents which is that our position remains very clear on this: There were a number of documents which Your Honours showed the witness which the Prosecution showed the witness and which were shown by the Defence. Our view is that none of those documents should be admitted unless the witness was able to identify them in a very concrete fashion, either because it was his signature or he was involved in the document or he received the document. Merely because a witness may be able to identify a name in a document or an event or the context, in our view, isn't sufficient to have the document rendered reliable. What is necessary is a form of identification. And that has been our position throughout. It is possible that a witness may well identify a name in a document but without being able to indicate in any way whether that document is reliable. If a document is to be relied upon as a record of facts, as a record which could contribute to the truth-finding process, in our view, a witness must be called who can identify that document so that, as we've said all along, the Defence or maybe the Prosecution is in a position to cross-examine on the record itself, on the information itself that is contained in those documents. And that's the principle which we would ask Your Honours to apply when looking at all the contested documents which as Your Honours are of course aware is a decision which still has to be rendered. I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. You have repeated what you've told us on endless occasions, and we understand your point. And thank you for reminding us of it. I should like to pass on to another subject before we call in the witness. So I would like to request the parties to take note of what I'm going to say. I'm going to say it slowly so that the interpreters can follow. I think they have been given the document. I'm reading what we wish to tell the parties. The Chamber invites the parties, which means the Prosecution and the Defence for both accused, if they so wish to provide clarifications on the two following points: Firstly, the Chamber notes that up to the present, the parties have not in their submissions in writing, including their pre-trial briefs, provided an analysis of essential legal elements of the crimes mentioned in the indictment. In the wish to be fully informed, the Chamber, therefore, calls on the parties if they so wish to express their positions in writing on this subject. Secondly, the Chamber notes that the indictment indicates, and I quote: "During the entire period covered by the present indictment, Bosnia and Herzegovina was the scene of an armed conflict." However, the Chamber is not aware that the Prosecution has taken a position regarding the nature of international humanitarian law applicable to this armed conflict. It is, we underline, in the aim of being fully informed that the Chamber, therefore, calls on the Prosecution if it so wishes to express its position in writing on this subject. Naturally, the lawyers for the accused may, if they so wish, respond in writing to any explanations provided by the Prosecution on this point. The Chamber notes in this connection that the lawyers representing General Hadzihasanovic have already indicated in their pre-trial brief that they are of the opinion, and I quote: "International humanitarian law applying specifically to international armed conflicts cannot apply" to the present case. Therefore, the Chamber is calling on the parties, of course, if they wish to do that, they're not obliged in any way, this is simply an invitation to them and it is up to the parties to judge whether they wish to or not, to provide the Chamber with clarifications regarding these two points that I have referred to. The first having to do with the elements of -- legal elements of the crimes charged in the indictment. And secondly, the question relating to international humanitarian law that is applicable to an armed conflict. Having noted, as indicated by the Chamber, that as far as one Defence team for one of the accused is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. concerned, the international humanitarian law that is applicable to international armed conflict is not applicable in this case. So I ask you with a clear head to read through what has been said. And if you consider it to be useful, to provide us your submissions in writing if you so wish. That is the second point that is now settled. We shall now pass on to the next witness. Does anyone have anything to say at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before the witness comes in, I should like to inform you that my colleague, Stephane Bourgon, has just left the courtroom. He didn't want to interrupt you. He's going to Sarajevo to interview a witness that has been called by the Trial Chamber. And the appointment was made by the OTP. We have advised the legal officer that there were certain problems in this connection. We wanted a legal assistant from our team to attend. However, at the last moment, the per diems were not authorised for our legal assistant. So the co-counsel had to leave. He will be coming and going twice this week. We feel that that is not economical. That costs the Tribunal a lot. And his absence is not legally justifiable. We do not wish to discuss this issue in court today, but as we are coming close to the end of the Prosecution case and in connection with the Defence preparations, we would appeal to the Chamber to support the Defence in their request for assistance so that our clients should have all the rights that are guaranteed to them and for us to be able to carry out all the obligations that have been assigned to the Defence team. Thank you for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Regarding this problem, we learn that the Prosecution is about to interview a witness in Sarajevo. We knew that last week Mr. Mundis told us that he had to go there. We don't know who is the person who will be heard or interviewed. And we discover that there is a problem linked to the fact that the Defence wanted to be present in person during the examination on the spot, that the Defence originally wanted to send one of its assistants. But due to matters linked to the financing on the part of the Registrar and the Tribunal, the Registrar would not approve the allowance for the assistant. And that is why you have had to send your co-counsel to be present during those proceedings. And you are asking for our assistance. As you know, and as I have said on a number of occasions, the Chamber unfortunately does not have any financial resources at its disposal with which it would be able to resolve such a problem. The only authority is the Registrar over which we have absolutely no influence. So the matter should be addressed with the Registry. However, in my personal opinion there was an absolute necessity for a Defence lawyer to be present so that once the witness comes to The Hague following an agreement reached and a decision of the Pre-Trial Judge, you still have the opportunity to meet this witness before he testifies here in The Hague. So I don't think it was absolutely essential for you to go there when you can see the witness later on. That is just a personal remark I have to make. And I'm speaking in my own name solely and not on behalf of the whole Trial Chamber. If I was to rule regarding the need for the Defence to be in contact with the witness, I think it is up to the party calling the witness that should interview the witness. I don't see why the other party should be present during that examination when the other party will always have an opportunity to cross-examine the witness later on. So anyway, that is a very -- purely personal remark on my part and that I wish to make. Of course, you will have the full assistance of the Chamber as far as its possibilities allow to make sure that the rights of both accused are respected. And unfortunately, your co-counsel has had to leave. Clearly, this will be a difficulty for you. But the very reason for having a co-counsel is because such a possibility should be envisaged, that one Defence counsel has to be present whereas the other one may be usefully employed assisting the accused. Madam Benjamin, do you have anything to say regarding these particular financial issues? Having noted that when this problem arose, the parties could have gone to see the Registrar together in an effort to resolve the problem jointly. Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have anything to say on this matter. But I do wish to thank the Chamber for the guidance that you have given to us, and we will certainly deal with it. Secondly, I wish to inform the Chamber in the manner in which I wish to proceed to the witness that is coming. My understanding from the request of the Trial Chamber is that this is a witness that is basically coming to inform us as to the running of the archives. And so, my intention is to have him deal with the role of the archives and the operation of the archives. I have indicated to my colleagues on the other side that that's how I intend to proceed. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The witness, who is an archivist, will certainly be able to provide information for us. In any event, I have brought the originals. And as we do have the originals, should the need arise, we can show the originals to the witness so that the archivist can inform us regarding elements of reliability that are so dear to Mr. Bourgon and to Mr. Dixon, regarding the signatures, the stamps, the registration, et cetera. So during the questions by the Judges, we will ask the archivist to give us his assessments on the indicia of reliability. So before calling the witness, has the Defence anything to say? I saw that you were about to stand, so I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you have already moved on to another subject, and I don't wish to interrupt. But related to the previous matter, I just wish to point out, the Defence is never present during the interview of a witness of the other party. This was an order by the Trial Chamber to the Prosecutor. There is reference to hundreds of documents which are of extreme significance to both parties, and especially for the Trial Chamber. In the interests of expediency, the Prosecutor said that they would not be able to provide us with written statements. So the agreement was that we should attend because the conversation or the interview would be videotaped. And it is the only occasion when the Defence has asked to be present during the proofing of the witness. Otherwise, we are fully guided by your instructions, and we do our best to rationally use all our personnel in the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just for the record I do wish to clarify that for Mr. Kubura, we have arranged for an investigator from our team who is a lawyer based in Sarajevo to be present during the interviews next week. So we have been able to take advantage of the Prosecution's offer. Because the timing was so short to have somebody present during the interviews, and she will be attending each of the interviews next week. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have 20 minutes to the break. So let us bring in the witness, ask him a few questions for the purpose of identification, have him read the solemn declaration, and then move on to questions. And I will give the floor to Madam Benjamin. No, no, I'm sorry. We have another five minutes left. Maybe it's best then to have the break to tell the witness so that he doesn't disappear, because he must be wondering why he has been waiting so long. He should be told that we had our own problems to deal with. And so we shall resume at around 4.00 or 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you bring in the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet the new representative from the Registry who has taken the place of the former Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one. Good day. I'd like to first check that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. So please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here by the Prosecution at the request of the Trial Chamber. You will be testifying about the BH Army archives. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you please tell me your first and last name, your date of birth and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Adem Omerkic. I was born on the 5th of February 1953 in a place called Priluk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Which town do you live in at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your position or what is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I retired two months ago. I retired from the military. I was an officer in the army, but I have now retired. I retired on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what rank did you hold when you left the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a major in the RBH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Had you reached the age to retire, or had you requested to go into retirement, or was your retirement involuntary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bosnia and Herzegovina, they were reducing the number of members in the army. In the federation army, 8.000 people have left the army, and they went before their time. I personally didn't want to leave the army, but I have fulfilled the criteria that have to be fulfilled in order to go into retirement. So I sort of retired on a voluntary basis, but in a way I had to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And are you receiving a pension now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't received a pension yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you will have a pension, won't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] God willing, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what sort of situation were you in? Were you a member of the military? And if you were, which unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a soldier in the Municipality of Stari Grad, which is where I lived. There was a municipal staff, the Stari Grad municipal staff. And my first position in the army, so to speak, was within a small detachment. It was called the Bascarsija detachment, and it wasn't in existence for very long. At the beginning, these things kept transforming all the time until we managed to organise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in 1993, if I have understood you correctly, you were -- you had a position in the Municipality of Stari Grad. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. It was within the Stari Grad municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to your position as an archivist, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my third time before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is your third time here. Do you remember which case you testified in, or do you no longer remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first time I was here was when the first four Bosniaks were put on trial, or rather, there were three Bosniaks, and someone called Mucic, I think he's a Croat. I'm not sure. Delic, Landzo, and Delalic were their names and there was someone called Mucic. But I don't know exactly whether that was his name. At the time I was a representative of the military archives. I was the chief of the military archives. On the second occasion, I had been called here by a lawyer -- well, I can't remember the case right now. Again, it had to do with the archives and with evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are telling us that you testified in the Delalic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that will bring back certain memories.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can see the lawyer Edina Residovic here. I was called here on the second occasion by her. I've just noticed her now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the situation is not unfamiliar to you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration now. The usher will show it to you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, you have a lot of experience at this Tribunal because this is the third time you are testifying here. So what I will now tell you is just to remind you of certain issues. You will first have to answer the questions that will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution. They are to your right. Their questions will have to do with your position as an archivist at the time up until your retirement. Once Ms. Benjamin has concluded her examination-in-chief, Defence counsel who are to your left will conduct their cross-examination. Once this stage has been completed, the three Judges who are before you, who wanted you to be called as a witness, will also ask you questions. I have a binder here containing documents that were provided to OTP investigators when they went to the archives. And we will certainly have the opportunity of asking you some questions that have to deal with these documents, that have to do with these documents. They are purely technical documents. They don't have to do with the substance of the case. These are just questions that are related to the documents since you held the position of an archivist. There are two other points I'd like to inform you of. As you have taken the solemn declaration, you are aware of the fact that you should speak the truth because false testimony could result in the prosecution of a witness. But there's also another point I would like to inform you. This shouldn't be applicable to you. When a witness refuses to answer a question, the Trial Chamber can compel a witness to answer the Chamber's question, but that in such a case you are guaranteed immunity. But this shouldn't be applicable to you. Try and answer the questions in a precise and clear manner. Since the proceedings are oral and your answers are important as we are relying on your testimony, if you do not understand a question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. You'll also have to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel, and they will certainly deal with the technical problems. And this should enable the Trial Chamber to become quite familiar with your work as an archivist. This is how we will be proceeding. And without wasting any more time, I will now give Ms. Benjamin the floor. Ms. Benjamin, you may start with your examination-in-chief now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major. Could you please state for the Trial Chamber your professional qualifications, please.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo. I studied comparative literature and library science. At the university of political science, I'm still enrolled at the university of political science. I'm doing postgraduate studies there, and I have one more exam to take at the university of political science, which is also located in Sarajevo. As far as my military education is concerned, as far as the military courses I attended are concerned, I have certain diplomas, but these are courses and in my opinion they are not of great importance for this Tribunal. They don't have much importance. I attended a course in SFOR, for example, and I received a diploma there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major, could you for the Trial Chamber's benefit tell us for how long have you been practicing as an archivist.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, I don't remember the exact dates, but it was from 1995, 1996 up until 2001. During that period, I worked as the chief of the archives and of the central military library. That's what my position was called at the time. That was the name of my establishment duties at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Prior to your duties before you retired two months ago, were your duties the same as when you testified here in 1997 and 1998? Were your duties the same as prior to when you retired?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: From 1991 - I don't know the exact date, though - I was transferred from the military archives where I was the chief of the archives and of the library. I was transferred to the administration for civilian and military relations within the federation army. I worked as an officer for liaising with the organs of power in municipalities and local communes, republican organs and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line -- page 36, line 9, it says "from 1991." As far as I understood, the year was 2001. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I also noticed the problem. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber for which archive you were responsible for prior to your retirement two months ago.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Just a little digression, I retired as an officer for liaison with the organs of power, so there's a slight time gap from 2001. So my memory might not be very precise as far as the dates are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. The last time that you practiced as archivist was what year?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 2001, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And for which archive were you the custodian?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the archives of the BH Army. The military archives of the BH Army because at the beginning when the army was established, we wanted it to be an army for the entire area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was its name. And whenever there was some sort of a mixed structure, we thought this was important because we were, I think, in an army that was fighting for the idea of Bosnia-Herzegovina's totality, comprising all the various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major, could you state for us what was the location of this archive.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: The archives of the BH Army changed its location from time to time. Its first location was in the immediate vicinity of the building of the Ministry of Defence. It was a small building, and circumstances were such that there was a fire in the archives. And in my opinion, the archives were preserved in spite of the damage caused by the water they used to put the fire out above all. And as I personally participated in the saving of the archives, it is my opinion that the essential archival material that we had at our disposal was saved. After that, we temporarily moved to the library of what is now the building of the University of political science. And we stayed there for a while until a building was established in the Ramiz Salcin barracks. That was the former Viktor Bubanj barracks. At the time of the JNA, the name of the barracks was Viktor Bubanj. We were provided with the necessary conditions for preserving and protecting documents. This is where we spent the longest period of time. And the third location while I was in that position, and because of the needs -- because the barracks were needed for other purposes, we were moved to Konjic, a small town which is about 50 or 80 kilometres from Sarajevo. We moved to a special military facility there. And I stayed there until I was transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying, then, that even though in spite of the fire, you were able to preserve all your documents? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's my opinion that the most essential archival material was preserved. Many things happened. It took a long time to save the material. It's quite possible that certain documents were lost. But I was personally present there, and since we later received reinforcements, help in protecting the material, I think that the important material was saved. Later, it was difficult to dry the material that was wet. This took a certain amount of time. Some of the material was damaged. But I think that the essential, most important archival material was preserved and saved.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, could you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what is the purpose of an archive. For what purpose are archives established?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of establishing a military archive is known generally speaking, but we as idealists involved in the defence of our state, when we were given the task of establishing an archive, naturally we received orders from the relevant command that it was our belief that this was our main task. We had to preserve such archival material which would be proof of our fight for a normal state in which normal people could live, and this was to be a place where we would preserve evidence on the people and the defenders of that state. And this is how we operated. And I told the personnel whose chief I was that this was a sacred task for us and that a positive version of history would be written on the basis of these documents. So we were moved by an ideal at the time. We wanted to preserve everything that could be preserved. So this was our ideal that prevailed. That was the main purpose, rather than the usual purpose of archival material. We didn't even think that it might be necessary for a Tribunal, but now we see it's necessary for a Tribunal, too. And what's important for an archive is to preserve documents, papers from various institutions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, Major, could you tell us within the archives of the BH Army, was there any particular -- any emphasis placed on any particular type of documents?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, we received instructions. We received a set of rules, and this was to govern our operations. We were at liberty to sort the material into various categories. For example, we had within category number 1 the most important material in our opinion. This category included material signed by commanders, for example, orders --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Before we go into the category of the documents, I was looking for general category. What type of documents were you responsible for preserving in the BH Army archives? And maybe if the Trial Chamber would allow me, maybe I can assist you. Did your archive concentrate basically on war documents or documents of a general nature?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, the material created in the course of the war, and it had to do with our army. And some of the material we had was material that was seized, for example. We received some material from the Ministry of Defence. And it had to do with documents of a general who is no longer alive. It was General Kukanjac who had a command in Sarajevo. That's where he was captured and so on. We had some of that material, for example, and we also had other material. So this is material that wasn't created within our units and our commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. So before we get into the documents itself, could you explain to the Trial Chamber the role of an archivist like yourself and what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: If I may make a general remark, it was my duty to organise work, the keeping and collecting and processing of archival material on the basis of a temporary regulation that we received from the main command within the framework of a document signed by the command. And pursuant to the provisions of those rules, we sought to abide by them as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So would these rules be -- would you be referring to the temporary book of rules when you say "rules"? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the temporary book of rules, yes. We had to be guided by that temporary document because we knew that the war was a temporary situation. So that temporary set of rules was probably modelled on some other rules, be they civilian or military. But essentially, we were guided by that book of rules. And it provided a framework for all our activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist us with the author of the temporary book of rules? How did this book of rules come into -- into the application of the archives?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: It came through the normal channels. It was signed by our commander, General Delic. And as we were in the central army archive, we received it through the regular military mail, through correspondence. It came as a certified and signed document with indications as to what should be done next with respect to the formation of the archives, the safekeeping, collecting, and processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. And now we move on to the area that you previously began to describe for us. When the documents come to the archives, what is your first -- what do you do first? When you receive the documents, what do you do first?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: We had a customary way of dealing with documents. There was a procedure prescribed for collecting documents. But there were cases when we happened to come across some documents by chance or we were told that there was some documents in a certain location. And it was wartime, and we didn't have normal conditions. There were shortage of electricity, water, paper, the quality of the typewriter ribbons was poor. But regardless of the way we found the material, we would group it, and then protect it from further deterioration. For instance, if the visibility or legibility was poor, if it was faxed and then the print would come off, you could notice it on your fingers, we would photocopy the document immediately and then attach it to the original and classify it according to subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get into the classification of the documents, we're talking about the source of the documents. And I think -- was the army obliged to send you documents? How did you source your documents?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: As this was the central archive of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the General Staff which was later transformed again, but through orders sent to subordinate units, we obliged them to send us archive material. And it was an obligation on their part to respect the deadlines, the method of processing, and to send us those materials as soon as possible. So we issued a number of acts that were, in fact, orders instructing subordinate units to keep collecting, safekeeping, and processing documents, and passing them on to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So now that we have learned how you source your documents, could you tell us how you -- the categories you put the documents in and how you identified the documents.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I already said that we had roughly four main groups, but the most important among those groups was the first group where we placed documents signed by the commander or the main commanders from the main commands and units. So these were documents that were orders, commands. Those were the most important documents in our view. Then came the second group of documents that we called reports. These were documents coming from subordinate units or units that received orders from a higher command. And then they sent reports following such orders. And these were reports mostly signed by subordinate unit commanders. So we had the freedom to make those categories and classify documents accordingly. The third and fourth group of documents were related to training, decisions, plans, I can't remember exactly all the details. But these were military documents. So to facilitate our work, we made these classifications. Then there was another breakdown according to commands, for instance. For example, we had the General Staff on one ledge, or the 1st Corps, and then within that the four groups of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what means did you use or what method did you use to assess the authenticity of the document?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: The customary ways. There were several things that were recognisable. Of course, first of all, there was the correspondence. Once the archive was fully set in motion, then the handover, takeover of documents was a kind of authentication because when a document was handed over, then it had to be logged and certified. However, other points of importance probably in all archives, we knew the heading, the form of the document, the signature, roughly. We were familiar with the stamps that all documents should have had as far as that was possible. Among those documents, there were frequent cases that we didn't have the original, but we had a photocopy of an original. But we kept even those because of the contents or because of some information they contained. And then we did our best to trace the original if we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So, Major, if I were to understand you correctly, there were certain characteristics that had to be present in a document before it could be considered genuine or authentic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And some of those characteristics will be the seal, the signature, and could you assist us if there were any more.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, for instance, in 1992, documents bore a red seal. And we knew immediately who the commander was for as long as there was this red seal. We later learned that it was a sign of authenticity. Because at first, I don't know if I may speak freely, the point was to prevent the so-called first column from infiltrating a document of their own. So this red seal indicated genuineness. I don't think there were many such documents. I think only in 1992 and the beginning of 1993. But later on, there were the blue seals when things became more developed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time may the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 133, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be placed on the ELMO, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that in my last contact with representatives of the Tribunal, when we were in Konjic, some of the archival material was taken for the needs of the Tribunal in The Hague. And it is my moral duty --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: We will come to that. We're coming to that. One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you put -- is it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Major, do you see the document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. If you had to look at that document, could you illustrate for us the characters you would try to pull out of it to determine whether it's genuine or authentic. And could we start from the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: We see immediately in the heading whose document it is, which command it comes from, the dates, the year, the square stamp which often we used as indication of authenticity, though we gave priority to the round stamp. But this administrative stamp indicating that it is the Ministry of Defence also meant a lot. It was one of the signs of recognition. Then to whom it is addressed, who the author is, and who the addressee. Then we also looked at the subject. From this heading, we see discussions on cessation of hostilities. Actually, we didn't analyse the contents as a whole because that would move us away from our daily duties. But as the head or chief, I always tried to learn what the text was about. As I lived in Sarajevo and I followed developments as much as I could, I think it didn't take me long to realise what the text was about. Then the capitals, the abbreviations which were mostly in capitals, and that also served as a sign of recognition. I see UNPROFOR here, then the HVO, then Central Bosnia, RBiH. All these are capitals that I would notice immediately. So that was also one of the ways of identifying the document. And then we knew who the main commander was, and we recognised many signatures, many signatures of commanders. So if all these details were logical, then we knew that this was some sort of an original document. But if one of those main elements was missing, for instance, a stamp, it would still be classified as part of the archives and as an original document. Also, if there's anything in handwriting, as on this document, this also helped us to recognise it because it would contain a signature or a message, and we had a certain trust in these elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So Major, ideally this document with the characteristics that you pointed out, this is basically what would be considered as an authentic document as far as the archives are concerned? This document would have presented all the characteristics that you would have needed for you to verify it is authentic or genuine?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: This document doesn't have some key evidence. It doesn't have a stamp and a written signature. However, in view of the fact that our intention was to keep archival documents, I would have taken this one probably and classified it among -- under the subject it belongs to. If it was a discussion of hostilities, as this one is, it wouldn't be in the first group but certainly in the second group. But again, it depends on the contents. This is not an order, so it wouldn't be put in the first group, but somewhere there even though commanders' documents were basically put in group 1. But it has quite a number of elements showing that it was drafted in our units, in our command, and even the event it refers to, as I was able to see by glancing through it quickly. But something is missing. Yet, I would keep it in the group, and that is probably what I did with this particular document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could the document be removed, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major, could you kindly assist us now with photocopies. When you received photocopies, what was the procedure in the archives? Did you attempt to find the originals? How did you deal with photocopies? How were they categorised?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Particularly at the beginning, it was my position that we must take care of all archival material. We would keep them in big boxes. And there were originals and photocopies and fax reports, et cetera, in those boxes. But my opinion was that all these documents should be carefully looked through, but this required a lot of time and we were always under pressure of other obligations. We had our regular duties to take care of. And I believe that we have managed to preserve quite a number of documents. There were some papers written by a commander on a piece of paper somewhere on the ground, on top of a hill or I don't know where. But we kept it. It may not have any importance, but we still kept it even though it didn't have a heading or anything. He may be saying "send such and such a unit up there." I can't remember all the details. But we would keep photocopies and duplicates until we found a particular place to put them in, until we saw that they were superfluous and an additional burden for our archives. But we kept a lot of these documents, and we were proven to have acted correctly later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. What is the procedure that is followed by the archives with respect to requests for documents at the archives? Did you dispatch your originals? How did you deal with the requests for documents in the archives? Generally first.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Do you mean requests from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Well, let us first deal with it generally. How would you deal with a general request, and then we'll go into the specifics of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Whatever we were under obligation to give to someone, I would receive an order from the commander, from the main commander of the army. He would say "to the head of the archives personally" or "to the archives, I order that for the needs of the Tribunal in The Hague or for the needs of a court in Zenica or anywhere else, reports dated the 5th of October, for instance, should be provided." So only following orders from the commander. So we would hand over archived material to individuals coming to look for it once we received the order from the commander. In most cases, somebody from the Defence Ministry could clarify any points that were not clear. That was the procedure. And that was the procedure followed when we had to give material to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, what would you give -- would you give the original, the authentic document, or would you give photocopies?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: We would mostly give originals or whatever it is we had. Sometimes we only had a photocopy. Then we would give that photocopy pointing out that that is what we have found in our archives. It is in the first group, but it is a photocopy, or it may be a document that it doesn't contain all the elements proving its validity or authenticity. So whatever we were requested to give, we had to give. In what form? In the form in which we had it. But mostly, it was originals that were requested, and we gave the originals if we had them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But earlier on in your testimony, you indicated to us that the major purpose of the archives was for preservation of the documents. If you give out your originals, I'm thinking, what happens? Do you make photocopies to keep in the archives? How do you deal with it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: In most cases when we give originals, we would produce photocopies and keep them. However, when the Tribunal was in question, the last time a large quantity of original archive material was taken from the military archives, we simply for technical and physical reasons were unable to photocopy all those documents straight away as they were so numerous. And so that brings me to what I wanted to say: The archived material taken in large quantities for the needs of the Tribunal in The Hague was handed over to the Tribunal in the original, in most cases. However, after a certain period of time the Tribunal returned photocopies of those documents. All the originals that were handed over were photocopied and returned to the military archives as photocopies, whereas the originals are here in the Tribunal. Because we were unable to photocopy them straight away because they were so numerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Major, how do you determine what documents you're handing over?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I would usually read this order. And in this order, it would be stated that you need to give such and such material to somebody who will be coming either from a military unit or a civilian authority indicating the date and the time when this person would come. And following the order, we would then hand over those documents to that person. And, of course, there would be a written receipt that would have to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong, would you not have to have some inventory taken?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Inventory? I don't understand. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would a list of the documents that have been removed be recorded?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there would be a list. For example, they would ask for an order from the 3rd Corps command, from the 2nd Corps command, or a certain report would be requested. There would be a list. We would compile a list. And on the basis of this list, it would be easier for us when entering the archives to find the documents requested in the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So in particular, the Tribunal, any documents that you would have handed over, you would have made a list and you would have been able to know whether it's an authentic document or if it's a photocopy that you would have handed over. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: When dealing with the Tribunal, all the archival material taken by the Tribunal would be listed by us, or rather Tribunal representative would compile an entire list, and I would follow this. And then the entire list of the archival material that had been taken would be signed by myself and the Tribunal representative. As far as the material that was important is concerned or interesting, we would usually provide the originals, and these documents would be listed. And it was clear that we had handed over orders, reports, et cetera, et cetera. So there were lists which had been signed. And the Tribunal and the archives would have these signatures, these list that had been signed. And even the representative of the ministry would have a copy because a representative of the Ministry of Defence was present in the archives. He was a sort of link between my subordinates and the civilian bodies. And naturally, he'd be a link with the representative of -- from this Tribunal. He was also present there and would sign a list of -- listing the archival material that had been handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And that list would be basically to verify or to represent that the documents listed were the documents that were in your custody, and they were original documents which you handed over. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, could the witness be shown document with the ERN 01062519, please, for verification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you put the document on the ELMO, please. In discussing the procedure that went on in particular with the Tribunal and the accessing of documents from the archives, you indicated to us that a list is prepared normally. Could you indicate for us on the document, and this is just an example, could you indicate for us the list on this document, please.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Is there something I should say?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a typical document that you just referred to? Is this how it's prepared?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is a good example. On the top, under the title, it mentions the relevant period, the year of the material that I signed. A representative is also referred to. And here, there's a reference to the documents that we handed over. It mentions a signature. This is a good example of how archival material was handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would the covering page be the receipt that you referred to? The top page, would that be the receipt that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The date is mentioned here; the period, from the 12th to the 13th. It says who participated in this, representatives of the Tribunal, of the ministry, and myself. My signature is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think we can remove the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And one final question, Major: Would you say that your archive, the archive of the ABiH Army, would have collected basically all the materials which existed during the conflict? And if not all, most of the documents?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I think that most of the documents were collected, although a significant part is missing. Above all, because of certain things that were the result of the war. I know that we had problems in certain units because there were no premises in which archival material could be kept. A lot of material was damaged because we didn't have the premises in which to keep them because the paper would be damaged by humidity, et cetera. And there were changes which occurred all the time, and as a result we didn't have the appropriate personnel for the archives. In Bosnia, we didn't have people who had been educated in archival science. There was a secondary school -- the secondary school in Sarajevo which -- out of which certain archival specialists would come out from time to time. But there are many factors which contributed to the fact that certain archival material was damaged. And perhaps certain people weren't aware of the fact that it was important to preserve archival material. Naturally, we attempted to influence them through orders, through persuasion, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now turn to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Omerkic. You have recognised me, but I'll introduce myself again. My name is Edina Residovic and I am representing General Hadzihasanovic in this case. I'd be grateful if you could answer a number of questions that have to do with the subject discussed by my learned colleague from the Prosecution. You've already told the Trial Chamber that you've appeared before this Tribunal as a witness, and you testified about archival material.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On both occasions, it was in the Celebici case; on one occasion, the Prosecution called you as a witness, and on the second occasion it was the Defence for Mr. Delalic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Recently, you gave two statements to the Prosecution, one on the 15th of March and one on the 3rd of June 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On both occasions, your statements had to do with free access on the part of OTP investigators to the BH Army archives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since I want to ask a question to the Prosecution, could the witness leave the courtroom for a minute since I have to ask the Prosecution a question given the answer that the witness has just given us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, you will have to leave the courtroom for a few minutes, and we will call you back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, I'd like the Prosecution to explain this fact to us. From the statement that the Prosecution provided us with dated the 3rd of June 2004, we found out that this witness told the Prosecution that he already testified on the 15th of March 2001 with regard to the archives. We informed the Prosecution of this yesterday, and we received a copy of the second statement in English. We are not asking why it wasn't provided to us at a prior date, given the obligations of the Prosecution, and we are not asking why the statement isn't in B/C/S because it's a very short statement. As a result -- since it was a short statement, we were able to inform our client of its contents. But my question is: Given that the witness in this statement talks about the fact that between the 9th of March 2001 and the 15th of March 2001, members of the ICTY had free access to the archives and they took from the BH archives certain documents, maps, various other documents that they copied. My question for the Prosecution is whether this is material that has to do with this case because when explaining the documents that the Prosecution has at its disposal, Mr. Withopf on the 27th of April informed the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution only had access to the BH army archives on two occasions, in the year 2000 in the month of October, and in the year 2002. No one mentioned access to the archives and taking documents from the archives in March 2001. And the witness testified about this, or stated that this was something that happened in his statement. So it is our belief that the Prosecution should first provide us with an explanation, and we should be informed of whether we have all the material that we need in order to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Benjamin, the Defence has told us the following: The witness allegedly -- according to Mr. Withopf, the witness was examined, and Mr. Withopf said that the OTP went to the archives and apparently worked within the archives and took some documents from the archives in the course of the year 2000. This was done on two occasions, in the year 2000, October 2000, and in the course of the year 2002. And the Defence notes that in the witness's written statement, the archivist said that in the year 2001, not in the year 2000 or the year 2002, the OTP returned to the archives and took documents from the archives. The Defence would like to know whether the documents taken in the year 2001 are documents that relate to this case, documents that they are not familiar with. Or the visit in 2001 perhaps had to do with another case and not with this one. Are you in a position to inform the Trial Chamber about this subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I became involved in this matter some 16, 17 weeks ago, and I'm not too familiar with what transpired before. But I do know that when I went to Sarajevo to conduct interview, I discovered that the witness had given evidence twice at a Trial Chamber here, and so I requested the transcripts be forwarded to me right away. And then subsequently I got the witness statement of which my friend alludes to. And I was told when I called that this apparently was investigations done for another case, and that the investigations that were done in 2002 or the seizure that was done in 2002. In 2001 was done for the purposes of this case, the one that was done by Mr. Withopf and company. That was done in relation to the present case that's before us. And I'm told that the one -- two or one was in particular in relation to another case. Mr. Mundis who I think would be more familiar, is not with us now. But if my friend wishes, I can investigate further and certainly let the Trial Chamber know. But I think that that was for another case, I'm informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Prosecution has told us that according to the information they have, if someone went to the archives in 2001, it had nothing to do with the present case. But Ms. Benjamin can't confirm this; only Mr. Mundis could do so. So this is something we could ask Mr. Mundis next week when he will be present in the courtroom. Is there anything else you would like to tell us? It's quite possible, unless the witness is mistaken, but it is quite possible that the OTP went there in March 2001 to investigate a completely different case that has nothing to do with this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I take note of the explanations from the Prosecution. But for the sake of the transcript, I would just like to point out that a representative of the Prosecution on the 27th of April 2004 informed all of us, and above all, the Trial Chamber, that they only went to the archives on two occasions, from the 11th of October to the 19th of October 2000; this is on page 6170. And on the second occasion, it was from the 15th to the 19th of April 2001 [as interpreted]; this is on page 6181. We wanted to clarify this matter. I will now continue with my cross-examination of the witness. And if my learned colleague obtains any additional information, I would be grateful if she could inform the Defence. There is a mistake in line 18. It's from the 15th to the 19th of April 2002, not 2001, which is what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I also noticed that, and I was wondering whether there was a fourth visit to the archives which would have made the situation even more complex. It's 5.25. We should have our break at 5.30. So it would be best to have our break now. And we will resume at 5 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor for your questions, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, you told us that you graduated from the university and from the department that has library science as a subject.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But before the war you never worked in an archives or library, did you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also before the war, you didn't have any experience with the Yugoslav Army, nor did you work for it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No, but I do my regular military service in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also before the war you did not work in the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Like any other citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the beginning of the war you joined the Territorial Defence, and as you told us you were engaged in the municipal TO staff of Stari Grad Municipality in Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, during the war, you spent some time in the military police, and then in the regional staff of the TO, and finally in the 1st Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: None of these duties had to do with collecting archival material, did it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you already told us, in 1995, sometime in 1995, you were appointed to the newly formed archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you took over your duty there, you found a certain number of army documents which needed to be categorised. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had no knowledge as to how those documents were collected or brought there which the archives had to register and categorise and preserve.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I would like to add that before I joined the archives, a former JNA colonel was working there for a short time because he had already announced that he would be leaving. And I was appointed by order from the 1st Corps as head of the archives. And when I came, this other gentleman left. They had started work on the archives, but they hadn't done much. There were lots of documents that had not been processed, and we continued processing this material, and we worked from then on as I have described.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were three other persons working with you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Neither they nor you had any prior knowledge regarding collecting and processing archival material. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: They worked there. They would work in the way their chief told them to. But these were the initial steps. It was only after my arrival that more organised efforts were invested. After me, another lady joined, and she was an archival technician. She had graduated from a secondary school which trained people in that field, though she was new there with no experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you started working there after you received an order from Commander Delic and after a temporary book of rules was adopted, and it was only then that you started in an organised manner to collect and classify the material.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But this was already after the war in 1995 and 1996. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I think that the war was still on. I'm afraid I'm not very good with dates. But I think this was before Dayton that the archives had been set in motion. An order had been issued to set up the archives, but I don't remember exactly when that was. But I think the war was still going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This order obliged war units to send a copy of all their documents to the archives. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've already said that the conditions for work in the archives were poor and that you were moved several times from the time you joined until you left the archives. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you were housed in the small building not far from the Defence Ministry which was destroyed by fire. Though, according to your testimony, many documents were saved, the most important part of the archives was saved, nevertheless many documents were damaged. And there was a certain disruption from the already-established structure of your archival material. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Let's say it is, though actually we acted according to the system imposed upon us. There were certain disturbances, but we believe that the most important documents were preserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From then until the present to the best of your recollection, the archives moved four times. They were accommodated in four different places, the faculty of political sciences, Ramiz Salcin, Konjic, and now the most recent accommodation is in the premises of the former military hospital.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: A small building next to the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a person dealing with archives, you can certainly confirm in court that transportation of tens of thousands of documents can lead to the loss and damage of documents and other problems which affect the value of the documents in the archives?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said that the first reason to form the archives were of a historical reason; that is, to preserve army documents so that one day one would be able to say what was going on during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I had to work according to the orders of the command. I was an officer, and I had to obey orders. And in my statement, I emphasised this. I was living in the hope that by these compulsory activities of ours, we would be doing something that would be meaningful, that would help to establish the truth regarding this unfortunate history that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The order by Delic was forwarded to units throughout the area under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I expect so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You acted on those orders, and I assume that some of your own documents were meant to speed up the execution of the order. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, though, at the beginning, now that some time has passed, it seems to me that no one took the archives seriously or sufficiently seriously, seriously enough. In Bosnia, even today, people somehow think that the archives are a nuisance and they can end up somewhere in the dump. And that is how people looked at it in the army at least. That is my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though Commander Delic's order indicated the deadlines whereby the archives were to be established, as the head of those archives, you knew that those deadlines were not observed and that new orders had to be issued, but the documents did not reach you precisely for the reasons you have now mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: That is true. Deadlines were not respected. Some documents would be forwarded; others not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you received some material, that material was usually not systematised or orderly for you to be able to file it into the archives immediately but you yourself had to categorise those documents according to the book of rules?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning when I was still very enthusiastic about it, I tried to save as much as I possibly could, and maybe I was an idealist. And I would accept even documents that were not adequately processed. There were such cases. But there were also other cases as the archives were running in, I would turn back a whole military truckful of documents because they hadn't been properly processed. And we were unable to do it ourselves as we were too few. Later on, our activities were expanded, and then we forced them to do their bit of the work properly. At first, there may have been some cases when we didn't strictly abide by the archival rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But another reason why the unit did not send you documents, and you referred to it to some extent, was that much of the army documents due to the war were lost, destroyed, or simply went missing. So the units couldn't send you the documents that had disappeared from their own records.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a question that perhaps needs a lengthy explanation. Whatever I would say would not be adequate because people who were assigned to the archives were not aware of what they should do or they didn't have the means to do it. Things varied from one unit to another. So that what would happen was that in premises where a certain unit used to be or a command, we would find it empty and no materials available. If we found some material, we would collect it and process it ourselves. But later on, we forced those whose responsibility it was to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once those materials reached your archives, did you mark it in any way so that you would know when and which document reached the archive?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: This was regulated by the handover-takeover. For instance, we found a box of documents with no notes on them or we would find four boxfuls of various archival material. Actually, whatever reached us was registered once the archives became more effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At first, and maybe even now, documents would be received in large quantities, several packages of documents from the 306th Brigade or the 5th Corps, so that when you receive those documents you were simply unable to log each and every document in that package. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: There were no cases when a unit would bring us documents and give them to us and say "here you are, process them." But archival material that someone came across that were not registered, I don't know how they reached the archives. Even before this archives was formed, I don't know what was going on. Obviously, archival material had accumulated in the meantime which hadn't been registered anywhere. They were just -- these documents would just be put in boxes, and what we did was to classify those documents and process them in accordance with the rules. However, there were no cases when somebody would come from a particular unit and give us documents and say "here you are, there were attempts to make us do it all ourselves, but we didn't have the time to do it."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, once a document reaches the archives of the BH Army, is it given some kind of a mark whereby it can be recognised as coming from the BH archives regardless of whether it will be taken from the archives or get lost or be returned to it? So my question is: Did you mark a document that reached you, mark it in a recognisable manner, or did you just log it into a book?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the logging of documents, we took the liberty with an ordinary pencil to mark these documents. And there were boxfuls of them. And looking through all those papers, we would indicate this is the 1st Corps. To speed things up. We weren't even aware that we shouldn't be doing that. But I said that we could use an ordinary pencil. This should be under group 1 in pencil, 1, 2, or 3, in pencil.
