So once we complete the reports from a particular unit, then we make a list according to how many we have. Sometimes a document may be missing. Then we would note it down on a piece of paper. We would just down the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, so these documents that are logged in the archival documents is -- are not marked in any particular way.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No. I would write down these numbers, though I shouldn't have done that either. But in view of the conditions we were working in, it made it easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You made reference to the red seal. Is it true that red seals in the former JNA were placed only on the most confidential documents bearing the designation of a state secret regardless of who drafted it and from what level? For instance, war plans and plans of deployment of units. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that the red seal was the seal of the former JNA and of the military secret. But before I became an archivist, I was told that I should trust only the orders signed by the main commander and bearing the red seal, which would indicate that it was strictly confidential so that nobody could plant a false document on us. Actually, both the red seal and the blue seals are authentic for me. But I think that the red seal, and I don't know who I learned it from, was the one that should be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you told us about the shortage of all kind of materials during the war, including the ink for stamps was in short supply. So, as you said, there were no rules as to which colour or what kind of stamp should be used for documents. Everyone did their best and used what they had.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I think the colour of the stamp is complicating things a little. When I said that there was a shortage of ink, I didn't really mention ink. But one could see that the text wasn't clear, the words were not clear, which meant that the typewriter ribbons were old so that the letters were not clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify my questions to make it easier for you to answer them. You told us when you receive a document, you look to see whether there's a stamp, whether there's a signature. And if you recognise the signature of commanders then these would be put in a more important category, shall we call it first or second category. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: All these key and recognisable elements were crucial. There wasn't one that was of primordial importance. The signature itself was not enough. When we had a stamp and a heading and many other elements of evidence, could we consider a document to be authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, none of you was a handwriting expert, and you couldn't claim with certainty that a particular signature belonged to the person indicated on the document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, it was up to you to judge whether a particular commander or chief of staff or some other person has signed the document, or that you believed had signed the document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document. This is P133, which you described. So I would like to ask you to look at that document once again so that I can ask you a few questions about it. This literature has the typewritten name of the commander, and it says here that it is certified by stamp and signature.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you make a distinction between a document like this and another one which would have in addition to the name that is typewritten, the handwritten signature of the commander and the stamp of that particular unit; in this case, the 3rd Corps? Would you attribute less importance to this document as compared to a document that would contain a signature and a stamp?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that a document of this kind which doesn't contain all the important elements like a stamp, handwritten signature in ink, we would classify it in the group it belonged to. When other documents such documents stored signed by the same commander, the same stamp, regardless of the fact that we don't see the signature here. I wasn't saying whether this is authentic or not. But I would put a document of this kind in the group it belonged to, and then I would search for the original with the stamp and signature and all the other indicia. That was how we worked. Because if I were to reject this, then somebody in the lower-level units might act irresponsibly. We thought this could be of assistance in finding the original with the stamp and all the other key elements required.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, when you received a document of this kind without a signature and a stamp, you would continue your investigations, and only once you found the original, that is, the document with a signature and stamp, would it -- you consider that to be the original of that document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in addition to the documents that reached you in the archives in the wartime military units for many years in accordance with your book of rules, certain documents were left behind that were kept in the units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. All the documents were not handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So some documents had to be kept in the units according to the rules for a certain number of years, and only after that time elapsed did it have to be handed over to the archives?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: For as long as this document may have been needed by the unit because it was more difficult to get the document from the archives. So I think it was the rule to keep documents in the units for about a year to be able to monitor the execution of orders. I'm not sure I can express myself properly, but I think that they had up to a year to keep the document in their own unit if that is where it originated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, all these requirements, when documents should be handed over, which documents, for how long they should stay in the units, all this was regulated by instructions issued by the army commander regarding the handling of certain documents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw this document a moment ago that doesn't have a stamp or signature on it, is it true that in the archives you didn't know why a particular document does not bear a signature or stamp, nor was it your duty to establish why that particular document doesn't have a signature or stamp? That was not part of your work, was it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. But we felt it to be our duty to seek out the documents or what was lacking on documents. We didn't have the time nor could we leave and go to the 3rd Corps or somewhere else looking for it. Though sometimes we did go to certain units to show them how they should work and how they should hand over documents to us. So how this document reached us, we don't know. It doesn't have the key characteristics needed, but we accepted it, and we continued looking for the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said if a unit failed to give you processed material, later on you would send those materials back to the unit to put it in order. However, is it true that you never expected or asked the units to tell you how they had come into the possession of those documents? That was not a question of interest to the archives, was it?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid the question is not quite clear to me. But later on, as the archives became more developed, we received documents which were listed. When we checked the documents against the list, I don't think that they would ever give us some other document that didn't belong to that particular unit. If they did, I can't remember now. But if they did, we would insist that there would be -- there should be a list, a list showing that you handed over this certain documents and that we received them. Actually, they were handing over documents for which they were responsible. In their units there was an archivist who had to make a list of those documents and hand it over to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you mostly collected documents or material that originated during the war, is it true that during the war there were frequent organisational changes in the army so that documents would frequently change hands going from one unit to another so that you don't know which unit was actually the author of the document; you just know who gave you the document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that there were transformations in units. For example, a brigade would first be called 1st Brigade, then two years later it would be called the 101st, and then towards the end of the war it may be called the 501st Brigade. So there were changes in the units. And we always contacted with the individual who handed over documents. And once we put documents on the shelf belonging to a particular brigade, for instance, the 1st Brigade, then as it changed names, we put 101st, and then 501st without entering into who the commander was. But still knowing that the documents related to a particular unit, regardless of any transformations that may have been taken place. It may be the 1st or the 101st. So we wanted to help future investigators in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, if I put it this way, you didn't follow the chain of transmission of documents from the time it was created up until the time that a given unit carrying out the orders of Commander Delic provided you with the document in question. For example, in Travnik, the 17th Krajina Brigade perhaps issued a document that you would receive in the archives in 1995. But would it be true to say that you didn't know how this document circulated, which units it passed through, whose hands it passed through until the time that it arrived in the archives of the BH Army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But in such a situation, it was important for me that the person who came to hand over such material to me in the archives was material -- this was material that I took charge of as original material. And all such material I considered to be material of a certain kind, although some of the documents didn't have some of the key elements required. They didn't have some of the key elements that an original requires. Sometimes it would be a photocopy. Sometimes something would be missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you would receive a document from the year 1992 or 1993, for example, when you had it in your hands, you didn't know who issued the document, who signed it, whether the person's whose name is mentioned is the actual person who signed it, you don't know whether the order was forwarded to a unit or not; in such cases you wouldn't know whether the unit received a document or not. All such important issues for the military are not issues that you in the archives could be aware of. You couldn't find answers to these questions when you received documents from units at a subsequent date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: The question is a little lengthy, and I'm not sure that I've followed you. In 1996 and later on, when we received such material, the quantity of material received was substantial. Among the material we received, when the material was delivered by a car full of material, I was interested in the certified list. Then I would check the order. And then we would proceed rapidly because at the time I didn't have enough time to examine all the essential characteristics. What was important for me was that I had a complete list of documents that had been certified by their commander who was in Tuzla or I don't know where. And then if there was a complete list of all the orders, we were able to proceed with this handover of documents more rapidly. So for us archivists this manner of proceeding was sufficient. So I couldn't examine the documents in detail as I did in 1995 when the quantity of documents handed over was not that great.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps we haven't understood each other very well. I'll try to put briefer questions to you. Do you still have the document, the Prosecution's Document P133 dated 26th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says that this document was issued on the 26th of January 1993. Would it be correct to say that you personally do not know whether this document was issued on the 26th of January 1993 or not? This isn't one of your tasks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also don't know whether Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. The name can be found at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But as an archivist have no personal knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you received this document in 1996 when the archives were created, you do not know where this document was from the 26th of January 1993 up until the time it entered your archives. You don't know the chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, you do not know whether in the meantime anyone added other information to this document or whether anyone amended or changed the document because this isn't an archivist's task. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Likewise, you don't know who from January 1993 up until the time that the document arrived in the archives, you don't know who had access to this document during that period?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. All I know is about the documents that I was handed over. These aren't things that I can answer because I don't know whose office it was in, which commander had given the document, et cetera. These are things I don't know. I know how I received certain documents. This is what I know. But as to what certain units had, I can't say anything about that. But I could tell you certain stories just like every other Bosnian could. I could tell you that a certain commander was in a given place, another commander in another place. I could engage in guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, you didn't know when a unit was disbanded or, for example, the 3rd Corps was disbanded? In such cases, weren't interested in who within those units preserved some of the wartime material of those documents. This isn't something you were interested in until the time that you received those documents.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Look, this was of importance to us. I asked my chief, my boss, to ask the commander -- to tell the commander that educated people should work in the archives, people who had a certain degree of literacy, people in a position to process such material. Because sometimes material could get dirty. It was wartime. It wasn't a gentleman's job, as they said in Bosnia. But we insisted on the fact that it was very important for us to have educated and trained people working in the archives. And we asked for good equipment, and they promised to provide us with more contemporary equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that when you received a document in accordance with the orders issued by your superior, you were authorised to allow people mentioned in that order to have access to the archives?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If someone requested access to the archives -- well, in fact, the commander would inform us of who would be coming to the archives, and then we were told to provide that person with access to the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that if there was a state request, request from military organs, you could issue documents from the archives if the commander ordered you to do so.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, you provided such people, such individuals with copies of the documents, and you would provide a statement according to which the original was in the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Well, if the Tribunal is in question, yes, we would provide a statement stating what the case was. But when certain civilians, people from civilian structures, for example, doctors, the police, et cetera, judges in Bosnia, when they made requests, we would make a record of this in a certain notebook. We would say on the basis of a commander's order, such and such a document was provided, and I would then sign this. This was the usual way of providing archival material.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the request of a state organ, a court, or someone else, you would also check to see whether the documents that they had in their possession were documents the originals of which you had in the archives. And you would either provide oral testimony with regard to this matter as you did in the case of -- in the Celebici case, or you would put this in writing?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did this very seldom, and it was usually in situations like the one I'm in now. It was at the request of the Tribunal, et cetera. That's when I would personally testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before this large quantity of documents were taken out of the archives, and my learned colleague has asked you about this, you would on the whole provide smaller quantities of documents, at the most about ten documents would be provided in the archives. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the year 2000, in fact, at the request of the Tribunal and on the basis of an order issued to you by your superiors, you gave free access to the archives for investigators from the Tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They examined the archives in the barracks that used to be called the Viktor Bubanj barracks?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: No, no. First of all, this took place in the Viktor Bubanj barracks. But the large amount of documents was delivered in Konjic. The archival material was kept in a military facility, and that is where we delivered this significant quantity of archival material. We had been in Konjic for a year or two, a year and a half, I think. And the archives was then relocated to Sarajevo. But when the archival material was delivered to the Tribunal, the archives were in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was in the archives in Konjic on behalf of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: In the document that I saw a minute ago, I think that the person who was involved in this signed this document. But I don't know the person's name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, these tens of thousands of documents that were taken from the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina were not taken from the Ramiz Salcin barracks; they were taken from the archives that were located in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. DO. That's where we were located. But the representatives of the Tribunal came to the Ramiz Salcin on another occasion, and that's where they took documents from as well. So the commander of the Ministry of Defence ordered that they should be allowed to take whatever they were interested in. I can't remember this exactly, but there's a record of this, documents that I have signed and documents signed by the minister of defence. And on the basis of the commander's order and an order of the minister of defence, archival was delivered on two occasions, the archival material requested by OTP representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now interested in Konjic. When representatives from the Tribunal came to Konjic, did they arrive with a list of documents that they were interested in, and did they immediately take away all of the documents that were kept in the archives?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC
utterances.text: They wanted to take away certain documents, and they were able to take whatever they wanted. A representative could say that he wanted such and such a document, and he would take it. They had access to everything, and they could take whatever they wanted, which is what they did. Similarly in the Ramiz Salcin barracks, the same thing was done. That was done on the basis of an order. Representatives from the Tribunal arrived with a translator, and they were given access to all of the rooms in which archival material was kept and they could take what they were interested in. For example, if they found in a binder, document 1, 2, 5, 100, it doesn't matter what the number is, in such a case we would immediately photocopy the original, we would leave the originals, and they would take the photocopies to the Tribunal. This was how we handed over material in the Ramiz Salcin barracks. But later on when they took even more documents from the Konjic archives, they took all the archival material, all the original material, but this was -- they signed for it. The Tribunal returned photocopies of these documents. They didn't return the originals. But all the photocopies were returned to the military archives.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15 minutes. Between 15 minutes and half an hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we probably won't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, try to proceed rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would again like to draw your attention to -- I would like to address an issue for which I would need an additional 15 minutes. We don't have any records or any statements according to which documents were taken in Konjic. As a result, would you allow me to continue for 15 minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have to continue tomorrow. Since we will have to adjourn, it will be best to continue tomorrow. You will require a full 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 15 minutes would be the minimum, and half an hour would be the most time I'd require. It depends on what the witness says because the witness has mentioned a fact that we weren't aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The legal officer will do her calculations, but I think you'll be going over time. But the Judges have questions, and I personally have questions for the witness. And as a result, it will be necessary to continue tomorrow. So it would be best if we adjourned now. Major, you will have to return tomorrow at 9.00. Unfortunately, you will have to spend the night in The Hague and we will continue with your examination tomorrow at 9.00. Madam Usher, would you escort the witness out of the courtroom. And in the meantime, you should not have contact with anyone. You should not have contact with either of the sides, and you shouldn't have any contact with the Judges either, who in any event won't be seeing you. You may escort the witness out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be best to adjourn now, and we will continue with the cross-examination of this witness tomorrow. As we have another witnessed for tomorrow, I would like to ask the parties not to ask the second witness the same questions. That would not be useful. Try to ask important questions. What is important is to know how the archives were organised and it's important to know how they dealt with the archival materials. Perhaps the second witness could provide additional information. But do not ask the second witness the same questions. These issues aside, are there any other subjects that either of the parties would like to address? Ms. Benjamin, anything else you would like to address?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Not at this moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No issues to be raised by the Defence? In that case, I will see everyone at the hearing tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of June, 2004, at 6.49 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.50 p.m.,
